title: Pappardelle al Ragù di Lepre
subtitle: wide ribbon pasta with Tuscan braised hare ragu
excerpt: Pappardelle al ragù di lepre is the signature pasta of Tuscany in autumn: hare braised slowly in red wine and aromatic vegetables until it falls from the bone, then shredded and served with wide egg pappardelle. Serves 6.
sourceNotes: Pappardelle al ragù di lepre is one of the most celebrated pasta dishes of Tuscany, particularly associated with the provinces of Arezzo, Siena, and Florence during the autumn hunting season for hare. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), gives a lepre in salmi (marinated hare) that forms the basis of most Tuscan hare preparations. Paolo Petroni, La vera cucina toscana (1984, Bonechi), includes pappardelle con la lepre as a central Tuscan dish. The hare is typically marinated in red wine overnight, then braised with a soffritto of onion, carrot, and celery and returned to a rich, dark sauce. Rabbit is a legitimate and more accessible substitute.

recipe.freezeNotes: The ragu freezes very well without the pasta. Freeze in portions for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch and freeze half. The ragu only improves after reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The hare should be marinated overnight. The finished ragu keeps refrigerated for 3 days and improves the next day.

glossaryTerms.definition: The Italian base of finely diced onion, carrot, and celery cooked slowly in olive oil until soft and sweet. It forms the flavour foundation of most Italian braises, ragus, and slow-cooked sauces.

European brown hare, stronger in flavour than rabbit and traditional game in Tuscan cooking. It is typically jointed and marinated in red wine before braising to moderate its gaminess. Rabbit (coniglio) can be substituted: reduce the braise time to 60 to 75 minutes and skip the overnight marinade.

content.text: Hare ragu is a two-day project: overnight marinade in red wine, then a long slow braise until the meat falls from the bone. The bones go in too; they enrich the ragu as it reduces. Cook a

of onion, carrot, and celery before adding the hare and wine. Once the hare is cooked and shredded, reduce the sauce on the hob until thick and dark. Tossed with fresh pappardelle, it is one of the great Italian pasta dishes.

Hare is more intense than rabbit and the overnight wine marinade is important for moderating its gaminess. If hare is unavailable, rabbit works with a shorter braise and no overnight marinade. Wild boar can also be used with the same approach.

items.prepNote: one hare, jointed by the butcher

content.text: Place the hare pieces in a bowl with {{red-wine}} of red wine, rosemary, bay leaves, and bruised garlic. Cover and refrigerate overnight, at least 8 hours. Remove from the marinade, pat dry, and strain and reserve the wine.
Brown the hare and build the ragu
Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large casserole over a high heat. Season the hare pieces and brown in batches until deep golden on all sides. Remove and set aside.

Reduce heat to medium. Add {{onion}} of diced onion, {{carrot}} of carrot, and {{celery}} of celery to the casserole. Cook for 10 minutes until soft. Add the reserved marinade wine and simmer until reduced by half.

Return the hare to the casserole. Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} of tinned tomatoes and {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock. Bring to a simmer, cover, and transfer to the oven at 150°C fan for 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours until the meat is completely tender and falling from the bone.

Remove the hare pieces. Shred all the meat from the bones and return it to the sauce. Discard the bones, bay leaves, and rosemary. Simmer the ragu uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes until thickened and concentrated. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper.

Cook {{pasta-fresh}} of fresh pappardelle in well-salted boiling water for 2 to 3 minutes. Reserve pasta water. Drain and toss with enough ragu to coat generously. Add a splash of pasta water if needed. Serve with {{parmesan}} of Parmesan.

items.cause: Marinade time too short, or marinade not drained
items.fix: A full overnight marinade is important for hare. Pat the pieces dry before browning to remove marinade residue from the surface.

items.symptom: Meat is tough after the full braise time
items.cause: Temperature too low, or an older, larger hare
items.fix: Continue braising at the same temperature until a fork slides in easily. Hare varies: some need 2 hours, some 2.5.
Simmer uncovered until the sauce reduces to a thick, dark consistency that coats a spoon.

content.text: is Tuscan autumn cooking, inseparable from the olive harvest and the hunting season that runs from September to January. In the hill towns of Chianti, Siena, and the Maremma, hare ragu appears on almost every trattoria menu during this period. It is a serious dish: labour-intensive, long, and dependent on good ingredients. The combination of the dark, wine-enriched ragu and the wide egg pasta is one of the most satisfying in Italian cooking. Outside the hunting season, rabbit ragu with the same technique and the same pasta is its year-round equivalent.
